Reading · the five-star problem

1.1 Discuss. When did you last read reviews before buying something or choosing a restaurant? Did you believe them?

KEY WORDS

genuine real, not false

a rating a score out of five

to filter out to remove automatically

a refund money given back

The Five-Star Problem

Almost nine out of ten of us read reviews before we spend money, and for most people a good rating makes a purchase far more likely. That is exactly why reviews are worth faking, and why so many of them are.

The trade is not hidden. Researchers in Australia found sites openly offering ten positive reviews for eighty-five dollars, and restaurants advertising for people to improve their ratings. Paying for reviews is illegal in most countries, and it happens anyway. It is known in the industry as opinion spam, which is a polite name for lying.

Most of the faking, though, is smaller and more ordinary than that. A café owner asks a regular customer to leave a review. The customer promises to do it and then forgets, which is what customers almost always do. So the owner asks the staff instead, or a cousin, or a friend of a friend — and at that point something that began as encouragement has quietly become invention.

The platforms are not helpless. Their software watches for patterns — twenty reviews from one address, a burst of five-star ratings in a single afternoon, an account that has reviewed nothing else — and anything suspicious goes to a team of people who look more closely. It works something like a bank checking a card payment. Some companies have taken fake reviewers to court and won.

None of which helps you at the moment you are standing outside a restaurant with your phone in your hand. For that, one test works better than any other, and it costs nothing. Read the detail. A fake review says the staff are very friendly and the food was amazing, because the writer was never there and has nothing else to say. A real one says we arrived late and they still found us something to eat, or the chairs are uncomfortable but nobody cares. Specific beats enthusiastic. If a review could have been written about anywhere, it probably was.

And read the bad ones. Most people scroll the five-star reviews and stop. The one-star reviews are where you find out whether the problem is the food or the parking.

Grammar · verb patterns

PRESENTATION

When one verb follows another, the first verb decides the form of the second. There is no rule you can work out — the pattern belongs to the verb, so learn them together.

A verb + -ing · enjoy · avoid · finish · keep · mind · suggest · admit · recommend · miss · imagine · I enjoy reading reviews.

B verb + to + infinitive · decide · plan · hope · offer · promise · refuse · agree · manage · seem · afford · He decided to make a website.

C verb + object + to + infinitive · ask · tell · persuade · warn · advise · remind · want · allow · get · He asked his friends to write reviews.

D after an adjective → to + infinitive: It's difficult to choose. after a preposition → -ing: I'm interested in hearing about it. worth → -ing: It's worth reading the bad ones.

Some verbs take both, with the same meaning: start · begin · continue · like · love · hate · prefer · I like reading / I like to read.

verb + -ing (A)

verb + to + infinitive (B)

verb + object + to (C)

I enjoy shopping online.

He decided to leave.

She asked me to wait.

We suggested asking someone.

They agreed to give a refund.

He persuaded her to stay.

He admitted writing them.

I managed to book a table.

They warned him not to sit.

ERROR WARNING

These three are the errors the coursebook warns about, and they are the ones your writing will be marked on:

We've decided leaving. ✗ → We've decided to leave. ✓ (decide takes to )

I enjoyed to meet your brother. ✗ → I enjoyed meeting your brother. ✓ (enjoy takes -ing )

I like be at home. ✗ → I like being at home. ✓ or I like to be at home. ✓ (never the bare infinitive)

After a preposition, always -ing: interested in to hear ✗ → interested in hearing ✓ · worth to read ✗ → worth reading ✓

Negative infinitive: not goes first. He warned him to not sit down. ✗ → He warned him not to sit down. ✓

Vocabulary · reporting verbs

PRESENTATION

A reporting verb tells you what somebody did with their words — not just that they spoke, but whether they warned, offered, refused or admitted. Each one takes a fixed pattern.

A verb + to + infinitive · offer · promise · threaten · agree · refuse · She promised to write a review.

B verb + object + to + infinitive · ask · persuade · warn · advise · remind · He advised us to read both.

C verb + -ing · recommend · suggest · admit · He admitted writing them himself.

D Negatives: not comes before to · They warned him not to sit down. · She suggested not going at all.

Two of these can also take that: He admitted that he wrote them. · She suggested that we ask somebody.

WHY YOU DIDN'T HEAR IT

Reporting verbs are almost never stressed — the content after them is. In I'd advise people to read carefully, the loud words are advise is weak and read carefully is strong. Worse, would shrinks to 'd and disappears completely before a consonant.

Writing · a review that sounds real

WHAT MAKES A REVIEW BELIEVABLE

The expert in Section 4 gave the test: a genuine review contains something only somebody who was there could know. Your review has three jobs:

Say what happened — one specific thing, with a detail. Judge it — but not only positively. Say who it suits — and who it doesn't.

5.1 Which sentence is believable, A or B? Say why.

1 A The staff were very friendly. B We arrived twenty minutes before closing and nobody sighed.

2 A The food was amazing. B The bread came out warm, which almost never happens.

3 A I would definitely recommend this place. B I would go back, but not with children.

What do all the B sentences have that the A sentences do not?

ERROR WARNING

Three things go wrong when B1+ students write reviews:

1 The verb pattern. I recommend to go early. ✗ → I recommend going early. ✓ · It's worth to book. ✗ → It's worth booking. ✓

2 Adjectives instead of facts. Amazing, wonderful, perfect tell the reader nothing. Every adjective needs a fact beside it.

3 Only good news. A review with no complaint reads like a fake one — which is exactly what Section 4 said. One honest reservation makes everything else believable.

PLAN

Opening — name the place, where it is, and your verdict in one sentence.

What happened — one visit, with three concrete details. Not a list of adjectives.

The reservation — one thing that was not perfect, stated plainly.

Closing — who it suits and who it doesn't.

5.5 Read the model. Then answer the questions below it.

MODEL

Chorsu Osh Markazi — go before eleven

This is a plov place near the bazaar, and it is the best lunch in the district if you can get there early. We arrived at ten past eleven on a Saturday and the queue was already at the door, but somebody found us two seats at the end of a shared table and nobody minded that we were three where there was room for two.

The plov is cooked in one enormous kazan and it runs out at about one o'clock, which tells you everything. It arrived in four minutes. The rice was separate rather than sticky, the meat came apart with a spoon, and the tea was refilled twice without our asking. Two people ate for 45,000 so'm.

My only complaint is the noise — the room is tiled and there is nowhere for the sound to go, so a conversation is hard work. I would recommend going with one other person rather than four, and I would avoid taking anybody who needs a quiet lunch. Otherwise, I would go back tomorrow.
